chapters: Ergodicity and the Maths of Ruin

units.t: The Sanctum Teachings. Episode two.
In this episode: Ergodicity and the Maths of Ruin, Fat Tails and Power Laws, The Evolution of Cooperation and Second-Order Thinking.
Part one. Ergodicity and the Maths of Ruin.
A bet can make the average player richer every round while making almost every actual player poorer.
Understanding why is one of the most important ideas in all of risk.
The bet that looks good.
A stranger offers a coin game.
Heads, your wealth rises by 50 per cent.
Tails, it falls by 40 per cent.
On average you gain 5 per cent per flip.
Yet if you play repeatedly with everything you own, you will almost certainly end up nearly broke.
The trap is a quiet assumption: that the average across many people tells you what happens to one person across time.
Ten thousand people flipping once gain 5 per cent in total, the ensemble average.
One person flipping ten thousand times follows the time average.
A system is ergodic when these agree.
Wealth compounds, multiplying rather than adding, so it is not.
Physicist Ole Peters argues economics went astray by treating such situations as ergodic.
The arithmetic of decline.
Start with 100 dollars.
Flip heads and you have 150.
Flip tails and you fall to 90, because 40 per cent of 150 is 60.
Reverse the order and 100 becomes 60, then 90.
One win plus one loss multiplies your wealth by 1.
5 times 0.
6, which is 0.
A typical pair of flips costs you 10 per cent.
Over a hundred flips, a typical player sees roughly fifty heads and fifty tails, leaving about 0.
9 to the power of 50 of their stake: around half of one per cent.
Meanwhile the ensemble average is 1.
05 to the power of 100, about 131 times the stake.
That average is real, but propped up by a tiny number of astronomically lucky players while nearly everyone else is ruined.
Ruin is final.
Suppose someone offers you a fortune to play one round of Russian roulette with a six-chamber revolver.
Across a crowd, five in six walk away rich, so the ensemble looks attractive.
But one person who keeps accepting survives ten rounds with probability five sixths multiplied by itself ten times, roughly 16 per cent.
Play long enough and death becomes a certainty.
Any strategy with even a small probability of total loss, repeated often enough, eventually meets that loss.
Ruin is an absorbing state: once you are bankrupt, dead or banned from the table, you cannot use the good outcomes that would have followed.
The average never gets to rescue you.
Betting less.
In 1956 John Kelly, a researcher at Bell Labs, worked out how a gambler with an edge should size bets to make wealth grow fastest over time.
He maximised the expected logarithm of wealth, which captures compounding.
In our coin game, staking everything gives a typical growth rate of about minus 5 per cent per flip.
Stake a quarter of your wealth each flip, and a typical player grows roughly 0.
6 per cent per flip.
The same favourable odds become an engine of wealth simply by betting smaller.
Bet more than Kelly and growth falls.
This also defends ordinary caution against the charge of loss aversion.
A 50 per cent loss needs a 100 per cent gain to recover, so deep drawdowns cost more than they seem.
Survival comes first.
The practical moral is simple to state and hard to live by: survive first, then optimise.
A business that grows quickly on heavy debt may look brilliant in average conditions, yet a single bad year can wipe it out.
An investor using leverage can be right about the long run and still be forced to sell at the bottom.
Warren Buffett's well known first rule, don't lose money, is usually read as a joke, but in a non-ergodic world it is close to a mathematical principle.
Diversification, insurance, emergency savings and modest position sizes all trade a little expected gain for a large reduction in the chance of ruin.
This is general information, not financial advice, but the idea holds: you only get the long run if you stay in the game.
The key idea: A bet can have a positive average payoff and still be ruinous to keep taking, because the crowd's average is not one person's path.
Part two. Fat Tails and Power Laws.
Some quantities behave politely, clustering around an average.
Others are ruled by rare giants.
Mistaking one kind of world for the other is how sensible people get blindsided.
Two kinds of randomness.
Fill a stadium with a thousand randomly chosen adults and weigh them.
Add the heaviest person on Earth and the average barely changes.
Repeat with wealth.
Add one of the world's richest people and they may hold most of the stadium's total wealth.
The average now describes nobody.
The writer and former trader Nassim Nicholas Taleb named the two worlds.
Mediocristan is the land of the bell curve: height, weight, calorie intake, a dentist's income.
No single observation changes the total meaningfully.
Extremistan is the land of power laws: wealth, book sales, pandemic deaths, financial losses.
One observation can dwarf the rest.
A useful test: is the quantity physically constrained, or can it scale?
A baker can only bake so many loaves, but a book can be copied without limit.
The bell curve's promise.
The normal distribution, the familiar bell curve, describes things like human height, measurement errors and many test scores.
It arises when an outcome is the sum of many small, independent influences, none of which dominates.
Its tails thin out astonishingly fast.
Each extra standard deviation from the mean makes an event dramatically rarer, so events many standard deviations out become vanishingly unlikely.
That is why you will never meet an adult three metres tall.
Under a bell curve, averages and past samples are trustworthy guides.
The danger begins when this model is applied to quantities that do not come from many small independent influences, such as market prices, which can move together in a panic.
Power laws.
In a power law, the probability of exceeding some size falls away as a power of that size.
Instead of plunging like a bell curve, the tail declines gently, which is why it is called fat.
Earthquakes follow such a pattern: each step up in magnitude is roughly ten times rarer yet releases about thirty times more energy.
When the tail is fat enough, the variance can be infinite, and with a fatter tail still, even the average is undefined.
Economist Vilfredo Pareto noticed in the late nineteenth century that a small share of people held most of the wealth.
The eighty-twenty rule is a loose rule of thumb inspired by his work, not a law of nature.
In such domains, the outliers are the story.
Black swans.
Europeans once treated 'all swans are white' as safe, until explorers found black swans in Western Australia.
Taleb borrowed the image for his 2007 book The Black Swan: outliers that carry extreme impact and are rationalised afterwards as predictable.
Consider a turkey, fed generously every day for a thousand days.
Each meal increases its statistical confidence that humans are benevolent, right up until the day before a festive feast.
Its confidence peaks when the risk is greatest.
On Black Monday in October 1987, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell more than 20 per cent in a single day, a move that standard bell-curve models treated as nearly impossible.
They were describing the wrong world.
Living with fat tails.
If extreme events cannot be forecast reliably, change your exposure to them.
First, distrust averages and standard deviations in fat-tailed domains, and ask what the worst plausible case would do to you.
Second, never assume the biggest loss in your data is the biggest loss possible: the next record may be far larger.
Third, cap your downside, through diversification, insurance and avoiding heavy debt, so no single shock can ruin you.
Taleb also advocates a barbell approach, combining very safe holdings with a small amount of exposure to large positive surprises.
This is general information, not financial advice.
The deeper habit is to ask of any risk, 'Which world am I in?'
because the right strategy in Mediocristan can be fatal in Extremistan.
The key idea: In some domains no single observation moves the total much, while in others one observation can dominate everything.
Part three. The Evolution of Cooperation.
Why would selfish players ever learn to trust each other?
A puzzle about two prisoners, and a computer tournament in the 1980s, revealed a surprisingly hopeful answer.
The prisoner's dilemma.
Two suspects are held in separate cells.
Each can betray the other or stay silent.
If both stay silent, both serve a short sentence.
If you betray and your partner stays silent, you go free.
If both betray, both serve a long sentence.
Whatever the other does, betrayal is better for you.
So two rational prisoners both betray, and both end up worse off.
Game theorists call this mutual betrayal a Nash equilibrium, after the mathematician John Nash.
It is stable not because it is good, but because neither player gains by changing alone.
The game was devised around 1950 by Merrill Flood and Melvin Dresher at RAND, and Albert Tucker gave it the prisoner story.
The same trap appears in arms races, price wars and shared fishing grounds.
The shadow of the future.
Everything changes when the game repeats.
If you will face the same partner tomorrow, betraying today may cost you their cooperation for weeks.
The political scientist Robert Axelrod called this the shadow of the future: the longer and more certain the relationship, the more cooperation pays.
There is a catch.
If both players know exactly when the final round occurs, logic says to betray in that round, since no future remains.
Then the second last round becomes the last, and the argument unravels backwards to the first move.
This is called backward induction.
So cooperation is most robust when the end is uncertain or distant.
Open-ended relationships, like those between neighbours or long-term trading partners, sustain trust best.
Axelrod's tournaments.
Around 1980, Axelrod invited game theorists, economists, psychologists and others to submit programs for a round-robin of the repeated prisoner's dilemma.
Some entries were elaborate, trying to model opponents or exploit their weaknesses.
The winner was the shortest program submitted: Tit for Tat, entered by the mathematical psychologist Anatol Rapoport.
Its rule was almost childishly simple.
Cooperate on the first move, then copy whatever the other player did last time.
Axelrod then ran a second, larger tournament.
Entrants knew Tit for Tat had won and tried to beat it.
It won again.
He described the findings in his 1984 book The Evolution of Cooperation, a landmark across many disciplines.
Why Tit for Tat won.
Axelrod found four traits behind its success.
It was nice: it never betrayed first, so it never started trouble.
It was retaliatory: it punished betrayal at once, so exploiters could not profit for long.
It was forgiving: after punishing once, it returned to cooperation as soon as the other player did, avoiding endless feuds.
And it was clear: its behaviour was so easy to read that opponents quickly learned cooperation was their best response.
Oddly, Tit for Tat can never outscore its opponent in a single match.
At best it ties.
It won by eliciting cooperation from many partners, not by defeating any of them.
Axelrod's lesson for life: do not envy the other player's score.
Cooperation in the wild.
Axelrod found striking evidence in the First World War.
Drawing on research by Tony Ashworth, he described "live and let live" truces along parts of the Western Front.
The same small units faced each other for long periods, which created a repeated game.
Soldiers fired in predictable patterns or aimed to miss, avoided shelling at meal times, and answered real attacks with prompt retaliation.
Commanders later disrupted the truces by rotating troops and ordering raids.
Cooperation needs no friendship in advance.
Strict Tit for Tat has a weakness: one misread move can trigger endless retaliation.
Later researchers, including Martin Nowak and Karl Sigmund, found that more forgiving strategies, such as Win Stay, Lose Shift, often do better when errors occur.
Reputations, contracts and courts all lengthen the shadow of the future.
The key idea: In the prisoner's dilemma, each player's best individual move leaves both worse off, and that stable trap is called a Nash equilibrium.
Part four. Second-Order Thinking.
Every decision has the consequence you intended, and then the consequences of that consequence.
The second wave is where most clever plans quietly fall apart.
And then what.
A city wants less traffic, so it builds a wider road.
Traffic eases at first.
Then driving becomes more attractive, more people drive, new housing appears along the route, and within some years the road can be as congested as before.
Transport researchers call this induced demand.
The first-order effect was real, but it was not the end of the story.
Second-order thinking is the habit of asking "and then what?"
repeatedly, tracing how people and systems respond rather than stopping at the immediate result.
The investor Howard Marks calls a related idea second-level thinking: seeing what everyone else sees is rarely enough.
Most poor decisions are not stupid at the first step.
They fail because nobody looked at the second or third.
When measures become targets.
In 1975 the British economist Charles Goodhart observed that statistical relationships used for monetary policy tended to break down once authorities tried to control them.
The anthropologist Marilyn Strathern put it best: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.
Reward the number and people find the cheapest ways to move it.
Call centres judged on call length may rush customers off the phone, and schools judged on test scores may teach to the test.
The social scientist Donald Campbell argued in the 1970s that the higher the stakes riding on an indicator, the more it gets distorted.
In 2016, Wells Fargo employees were found to have opened accounts customers had not authorised, under pressure to meet sales targets.
Incentives that backfire.
The story goes that British officials in Delhi offered a bounty for dead cobras.
People began breeding cobras for the reward, and when the bounty ended, they released their worthless snakes, leaving more cobras than before.
The tale is widely told but possibly embellished, with little firm documentation.
A better-documented parallel is colonial Hanoi in the early twentieth century, where a bounty on rat tails reportedly led some people to release tailless rats to keep breeding.
Whatever the details, the pattern is real.
In 1936 the sociologist Robert K. Merton described the unintended consequences of purposeful action, partly caused by focusing so hard on the goal that side effects are ignored.
They are not always bad, but the more complex the system, the more of them there are.
Chesterton's fence.
The writer G. K. Chesterton offered a parable in his 1929 book The Thing.
A reformer finds a fence across a road for no apparent reason and wants it torn down.
A wiser reformer, Chesterton suggested, would say: go and find out why it was built, and only then may you remove it.
The point is not that every old rule deserves to survive.
Many fences really are pointless.
The point is that the reason for something is often invisible precisely because it is working.
A fence that keeps cattle off a road prevents accidents nobody sees.
In organisations, odd procedures sometimes encode hard-won lessons from past failures.
Removing them without understanding can reintroduce the very problem they quietly solved.
Thinking two steps ahead.
You can practise second-order thinking deliberately.
Ask "and then what?"
at least twice, following the chain past the obvious first result.
Ask how each affected group will respond, especially people with incentives to game your new rule.
Consider time horizons: many choices feel good in ten minutes and bad in ten years, or the reverse, like exercise and saving.
When designing a measure, pair it with others that are hard to game together, and watch what people actually do, not only the numbers.
Before deleting an old rule, look for its forgotten purpose.
Finally, stay humble: in complex systems you will still miss things, so prefer reversible experiments, small pilots and quick feedback.
The goal is not perfect foresight.
It is to stop being surprised by what was foreseeable.
The key idea: Second-order thinking means asking what happens after the obvious result, tracing how people and systems respond to a change.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. When is a system called ergodic?
Answer. When its ensemble average equals its time average.
Question two. In the stadium thought experiment, why does adding a billionaire change things so much more than adding the heaviest person?
Answer. Wealth can scale without limit, but body weight cannot.
Question three. In a single prisoner's dilemma, why do rational players both betray?
Answer. Betrayal is the better move whatever the other player does.
Question four. Why can building a wider road fail to reduce congestion in the long run?
Answer. Easy driving draws more drivers, called induced demand.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
